items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: PNPM for Beginners: Faster Installs and a Disk That Stops Filling Up
items.summary: PNPM is a package manager for JavaScript that installs dependencies faster than npm and uses far less disk space. If you have ever looked at your node_modules folder and wondered why every project has its own copy of the same packages, PNPM is the answer. It stores each package once, on your disk, and links it into every project that needs it. The idea is a content-addressable store. When you install React, PNPM downloads it once and keeps it in a global store. Every project that uses React gets a hard link to that one copy, instead of its own duplicate. The result: installs are faster, because most packages are already on your disk, and your disk stops filling up with ten copies of the same library. Using it is almost identical to npm: npm install -g pnpm pnpm install pnpm add react pnpm run dev The commands are the same, so switching costs almost nothing. The difference is under the hood: PNPM creates a strict node_modules layout where a package can only access the dependencies it actually declared. That sounds like a detail, but it catches a real class of bugs — code that accidentally imports a package it never declared, which works on your machine and breaks in CI. PNPM also ha

items.title: Bun for Beginners: JavaScript's All-in-One Runtime, Bundler, and Test Runner
items.summary: Bun is a JavaScript runtime that wants to replace three tools at once: Node.js, your bundler, and your test runner. It is written in Zig, it starts fast, and it runs JavaScript and TypeScript directly — no build step for most code. If Node.js feels slow to start and your toolchain feels like five tools taped together, Bun is worth a look. The pitch is speed and simplicity. Bun starts in milliseconds, installs packages faster than npm, and runs TypeScript out of the box. A small server looks like this: // server.js Bun.serve({ port: 3000, fetch(req) { return new Response("Hello from Bun!"); }, }); Run it with bun run server.js and you have a working server. No framework, no build step, no configuration. Bun also has a built-in bundler (bun build), a test runner (bun test with Jest-compatible syntax), and a package manager (bun install) that is noticeably faster than npm on large projects. Bun is compatible with most Node.js APIs and most npm packages, so you can usually drop it into an existing project and see if it works. items.title: Storybook for Beginners: Build Your UI Components in Isolation
items.summary: Storybook is a tool that lets you build and test your UI components one at a time, outside your app. Instead of clicking through five screens to see a button in its loading state, you open Storybook, pick the button, and switch it to loading with one click. It turns UI development from a maze into a catalogue. The idea is simple: every component gets a story, which is a small file that renders the component with specific props. A button gets stories for its default, disabled, loading, and large variants. A card gets stories for short text, long text, and no image. You see them all in one place, in a browser, with controls to change the props live. A first Storybook story looks like this: // Button.stories.js import { Button } from './Button'; export default { title: 'Components/Button', component: Button, }; export const Primary = { args: { label: 'Save', primary: true }, }; export const Disabled = { args: { label: 'Save', disabled: true }, }; Open Storybook and you can flip between Primary and Disabled, change the label in the controls panel, and see the result instantly. items.title: Prettier for Beginners: Stop Arguing About Code Formatting Forever
items.summary: Prettier is an opinionated code formatter. You run it, and your code comes out formatted the same way every time — same indentation, same quotes, same line breaks. No configuration debates, no style arguments in code review, no diffs full of whitespace changes. It is the closest thing JavaScript has to a solved problem. The idea is radical in its simplicity: Prettier does not ask what style you like. It has one style, and you accept it. That sounds restrictive until you realize how much time teams waste arguing about semicolons, trailing commas, and line length. Prettier ends those arguments by removing the choice entirely. Using it is one command: npm install --save-dev prettier npx prettier --write . That reformats every file in your project. Add it to your editor so it formats on save, and add a check to your CI so unformatted code never merges. The configuration file is optional — most teams use the defaults, and the only settings people commonly change are singleQuote and semi. Prettier works with JavaScript, TypeScript, CSS, HTML, JSON, Markdown, and more. It does not check your logic — that is a linter's job. Prettier only cares about how the code looks. items.title: Jest for Beginners: Testing Your JavaScript Without the Setup Pain
items.summary: Jest is the testing framework that made JavaScript testing feel easy. Built by Facebook for React, it now tests almost anything written in JavaScript or TypeScript — and it works out of the box, with no configuration, for most projects. If you have been avoiding tests because setup looked painful, Jest is the place to start. The pitch is simple: write a test file, run npx jest, and get a clear pass-or-fail report. Jest finds your test files automatically, runs them in parallel, and gives you a summary with the exact line that failed. It also includes mocking, code coverage, and snapshot testing in the box — features that other frameworks make you install separately. A first Jest test looks like this: // sum.js function sum(a, b) { return a + b; } module.exports = sum; // sum.test.js const sum = require('./sum'); test('adds 1 + 2 to equal 3', () => { expect(sum(1, 2)).toBe(3); }); test('adds negative numbers', () => { expect(sum(-1, -2)).toBe(-3); }); Run npx jest and you get two green checkmarks. items.title: A camp kitchen water and fuel planner in 60 lines of vanilla JS
items.summary: Packing water for a camping trip is a small estimation problem that most people solve by guessing. This post walks through a tiny planner that turns the guess into arithmetic you can see and change: no framework, no build step, about 60 lines of JavaScript. The model Water use on a car-camping trip splits into four line items, and each one scales differently: Drinking: people × days × weather Cooking: people × days × hot meals Dishes: days × hot meals (the whole group shares the bins) Hand washing: people × days That difference is the whole point of the tool. Drinking water grows with head count, but dish water mostly grows with the number of meals you cook. For a short trip with a small group, dishes can be the largest line, which is not what people expect. Fuel is simpler: burner minutes per hot meal, times meals, divided by how long one canister lasts on your stove. Every coefficient is an input field with a default: Drinking water, L per person per day The defaults are rules of thumb. items.summary: Reliable HTTP cron and delayed-job scheduling with automatic retries and full run logs — delay.run You've set up a Stripe webhook endpoint, sent a test event, and your logs say: No signatures found matching the expected signature for payload. Are you passing the raw request body you received from Stripe? The second sentence is the hint, and it's right most of the time. Stripe signs the exact bytes of the request body. If your framework parses the JSON and you verify the re-serialised version, or you use a secret from a different endpoint, the signature can't match. Here are the causes in order of how often they happen, and how to check for each. Stripe sends a Stripe-Signature header like t=1731571200,v1=5257a8.... To verify, the library computes an HMAC-SHA256 of "{t}.{raw body}" using your endpoint's signing secret (whsec_...) and compares it with v1. If even one byte of the body differs (a space, key order, a Unicode escape, a newline), the HMAC is completely different. There's no "close enough". By far the most common. items.title: How to Fix EADDRINUSE: Address Already in Use on Windows, Linux & Docker
items.summary: Originally published at umutgungorr.com. A practical step-by-step playbook to diagnose and cleanly resolve EADDRINUSE port conflicts across Windows, Linux, macOS, and Docker containers. When starting a Node.js, Python, or Vite dev server throws Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000, the OS kernel is telling you another socket or lingering child process already holds that TCP port. Blindly killing a single PID often fails because a supervisor like nodemon, PM2, systemd, or Docker respawns the worker immediately—or docker-proxy masks which container actually owns the port. Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000 at Server.setupListenHandle [as _listen2] (node:net:1904:16) at listenInCluster (node:net:1961:12) You can inspect the owning PID on all three operating systems with built-in commands. Checking the parent process (PPID / ParentProcessId) prevents killing a child worker only to watch its supervisor respawn it. # Linux / macOS (port 3000) lsof -i :3000 -n -P ss -tulpn | grep :3000 # Windows PowerShell (port 3000 + proses adı + üst proses) Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 3000 | Select-Object LocalPort, State, OwningProcess Get-CimInstance Win3

items.summary: Two silent failures from one layout change, and a short fix for each. Hi Everyone! This week I built a tool that turns YouTube videos into transcripts. You can give it single videos, but the useful part is giving it a whole channel or playlist. So before any transcript work, it has to answer a simple question: which videos are in this list? items.title: TypeScript `Type Predicates` on Arrays: Writing `filter` Calls That Actually Narrow the Element Type
items.summary: TypeScript Type Predicates on Arrays: Writing filter Calls That Actually Narrow the Element Type This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review. TypeScript's control flow analysis narrows types brilliantly within an if block. Check for undefined, and the variable becomes non-nullable inside the branch. Test typeof x === "string", and TypeScript knows the value is a string. Developers who rely on this behavior in conditional logic often assume the same narrowing applies to Array.filter(). The compiler sees the predicate callback, sees the check inside it, and returns the narrowed type. That assumption breaks the moment the filtered array gets used. array.filter returns original union type instead of narrowed type The filtered array still has the original union type because TypeScript treats the filter callback as a boolean function. The type system does not infer that a true return means the element matches a specific type. items.title: Mastering Graceful Shutdown in Node.js: Prevent Data Loss in Production
items.summary: What Is a Graceful Shutdown? Graceful shutdown in Node.js is the process of stopping an application server cleanly without interrupting ongoing user requests or damaging active database operations. Instead of instantly killing the application process when a stop command is issued, the server stops accepting new incoming traffic, finishes processing current HTTP requests, closes database connections properly, and then exits safely. This process guarantees that active users do not experience sudden network errors and that pending write operations complete successfully. Imagine a busy restaurant reaching its closing hour at 10:00 PM. The management does not turn off the dining room lights and kick paying customers out in the middle of their meals. Instead, the host locks the front door to prevent new diners from walking in, while the kitchen continues cooking orders for guests who are already seated. Once every remaining customer finishes eating, pays their bill, and leaves, the staff cleans up, turns off the stoves, and locks the building. items.title: Stop Renting Your Business Data: The Case for Serverless Invoicing
items.summary: Every month, thousands of freelancers pay a 'convenience tax' to SaaS providers to host simple PDF documents on a remote server. From an engineering perspective, this is absurd. Why are we offloading sensitive financial PII to a third-party cloud simply to generate a document that is fundamentally local in nature? When we started Vanza Invoices, we weren't just building a tool; we were challenging the assumption that 'connected' means 'useful.' By moving to an offline-first architecture using React and Capacitor, we eliminated the need for a backend entirely. Here is why the serverless paradigm is the ultimate security and performance upgrade for utility-based software. When you build a SaaS invoicing platform, you become a custodian of your users' most sensitive data: tax IDs, bank details, and client lists. Every database entry is a potential liability. If you store this data, you are responsible for it. You need SOC2 compliance, you need to worry about SQL injection, and you need to manage the inevitable data leaks that plague cloud-based providers. items.title: Gate features at compile time: a Roslyn source generator for Keyright entitlements
items.summary: Entitlement checks have a way of multiplying. One feature needs export.pdf, another needs reports.scheduled, a third needs a seats limit — and each one grows its own little block of "resolve the license, read the entitlement, decide what to do on failure." Copy that block around a codebase and it drifts: one call site throws, another returns false, a third forgets to check at all, and somewhere a string literal says exprot.pdf and silently denies a feature to every paying customer. The checks are individually trivial and collectively a liability. This is exactly the kind of repetitive, error-prone, mechanical code a Roslyn source generator exists to remove. Instead of writing the guard, you declare the gate with an attribute and let the generator emit a correct, uniform guard at compile time — and, because the generator sees your whole compilation, it can validate every entitlement name against your declared catalog and fail the build on a typo. This post builds that generator against the Keyright SDK. items.title: Segurança em aplicações .NET na era da IA: o prompt que eu uso para revisar código
items.summary: Peça para um assistente de IA: "crie um endpoint que retorna o pedido pelo id". Em segundos você tem um código limpo, compilando e funcionando. E, na maioria das vezes, com uma falha clássica: qualquer usuário logado consegue ler o pedido de qualquer outro usuário, só trocando o número na URL. A IA não errou. Ela fez exatamente o que foi pedido: algo que funciona. Segurança raramente está no pedido, e o modelo otimiza para o caminho feliz. O problema é que hoje se escreve muito mais código, muito mais rápido, e se lê bem menos do que se escreve. É o que eu repito para os clientes da Dotcode: IA amplifica o processo que já existe. Se o seu processo de desenvolvimento não tem segurança, a IA não resolve isso. Ela escala a vulnerabilidade na mesma velocidade em que escala a entrega. Neste artigo eu mostro as sete falhas que mais vejo em código gerado por IA em .NET, com o código vulnerável e o corrigido lado a lado, um programa que ataca as duas versões e, principalmente, o prompt que eu uso para fazer a IA revisar código com foco em segurança. items.summary: Your dashboard says a product has thousands of reviews. You trace the tile back to the review rows you just imported, and the arithmetic looks perfectly respectable. The unit is wrong. items.title: Building a read-aloud screen: phrases, tappable words and a finger that drifts
items.summary: Background A lot of what I read is still on paper: letters from the bank, school handouts, a recipe, a library book. I often want to listen to them instead, and I want to follow the words while I listen, so my eyes have something to hold on to. So I built Outloud Reader. You take a photo of a printed page (or open a PDF, or paste text), the app reads it out loud, and the phrase being spoken is highlighted on screen. It runs on iOS and Android, and it can translate a page before reading it. This post is about the reading screen, the part people look at for minutes at a time. It turned out to be the hardest screen in the app to get right. Word-by-word highlighting, like karaoke. It is still in the code as an option, but it was exhausting to watch. items.title: Shifting Compute to the Client: Architecture and Advantages of Zero-Backend File Utilities
items.summary: As frontend developers, we are often tasked with implementing deterministic data transformations—file encoding, metadata parsing, or deterministic hashing. The conventional approach involves a REST API round-trip: Upload (Blob) -> Cloud API (Node.js/Python) -> Processing -> Download (Result Blob). This architecture has substantial downsides: unnecessary network bandwidth utilization, server compute cost for standard operations, and a complex security model that relies on legal privacy policies rather than architectural enforcement. Standard file format conversions are the perfect candidate for native, client-side execution. Modern browsers now offer a robust local processing stack: FileReader and Blob APIs: Handle raw file input and output deterministically within local memory. HTML5 Canvas: Execute hardware-accelerated image decoding and re-encoding. WebAssembly (WASM): Port high-performance, complex C/C++ deterministic libraries to run natively on the user's hardware. items.summary: I wanted a Spotify controller on my desktop that I'd actually enjoy looking at. Not another flat grey box, but something closer to Apple's liquid glass: clear, soft, a little bit alive. So I built one for Windows. It's written in C# with WPF on .NET 8, and it's open source. / glass-player Glass Player A liquid-glass mini player for Spotify on Windows. Late-night vinyl, under glass: a tiny desktop widget that takes its colour from whatever you're listening to. Highlights Real frosted glass. The widget blurs whatever sits behind it with its own blur engine: clean 30 px corners, a thick bright rim, a soft lens ring and a faint pink/cyan refraction fringe. The cover sets the mood. One accent colour is pulled from each album cover and carried through the play button, progress line, glow and dots. Every song re-themes the card. A record that plays. items.title: ValueTask vs Task Allocation Traps
items.summary: While reviewing a high-throughput microservice profiler session, I noticed constant Gen0 garbage collection spikes. Tracing the allocations revealed an unexpected culprit: Task . When a method is marked async and returns a Task , the C# compiler generates a state machine. Even if your code hits a memory cache and returns a result immediately (synchronously), the runtime still allocates a Task object on the heap to satisfy the method signature. public async Task GetAsync(int id) { if (_cache.TryGetValue(id, out var u)) return u; return await _db.QueryAsync(id); } public async ValueTask GetAsync(int id) { if (_cache.TryGetValue(id, out var u)) return u; return await _db.QueryAsync(id); } Zero Heap Allocations: ValueTask is a stack-allocated struct that wraps either a result or a standard Task, avoiding heap overhead on synchronous completions. Reduced GC Cycles: Eliminating millions of short-lived Task objects drastically reduces Gen0 garbage collector pauses under load. Seamless Integration: It integrates directly into standard await workflows without changing downstream calling code. A ValueTask wraps a pooled or unpooled state and can only be consumed once. items.title: Decompile against the exact dependency versions: resolve references from a NuGet lockfile in Glass.NET
items.summary: A decompiler earns your trust one reference at a time. Open an assembly that stands entirely on its own and the C# comes back clean. Open a real one — a service that leans on a dozen NuGet packages — and the quality of the reconstruction suddenly depends on something outside the file you opened: can the decompiler find the referenced assemblies, and the right versions of them? When it can't, the symptoms are familiar. A method returns JToken but the decompiler won't expand the type or follow it to its base. An overload that differs only by a parameter type from a dependency resolves to // unresolved or the wrong candidate. Go-to-definition on an external symbol dead-ends. None of this is Glass guessing badly — it is Glass being honest that a reference it can't load is a reference it can't see through. Glass.NET — the free, strictly static .NET decompiler — closes that gap by reading your packages.lock.json. The lockfile is the one artifact that says, authoritatively, which exact package versions your project restored. Hand it to Glass and every external reference resolves to the assembly that really shipped, not an approximation. A compiled assembly does not embed its dependencies.

items.summary: NSCollectionView 有 4 種排版： 排版 1：1 個 Cell（1） 排版 2：2 個 Cell（2） 排版 3：3 個 Cell（1 + 2） 排版 4：5 個 Cell（2 + 3） 畫面目前有 5 個 Cell，使用排版 4（2 + 3） 使用者點擊第一排右側的 Close Button Cell 被刪除，排版依剩餘 Cell 數量重新切換 使用者立即點擊原本的位置 該位置明明有 Close Button，卻沒有觸發刪除 停頓一小段時間後，又可以正常點擊 使用 deleteItems(at:) 刪除 Cell，沒有呼叫 reloadData 只有排版改變時，才會發生點擊後沒有刪除的情況 把 deleteItems(at:) 改成每次都 reloadData，反而每次刪除後都會發生 prepareForReuse 沒有遺漏重置資料 刪除 Cell 時，main thread 上沒有耗時的工作 多次嘗試沒有結果後，改從滑鼠事件本身調查。我請 AI 加入更完整的 Debug Log，觀察： mouseDown 事件實際由哪個 Button 接收 mouseUp 事件的流向 NSEvent.clickCount 的變化 滑鼠目前位置透過 Hit Test 找到的 View 把過濾後的 Log 貼給 AI，能快速分析出情況，節省時間。 快速連續點擊時，Log 出現了一個很特別的現象：clickCount 持續增加，但接收 mouseDown 的 Button 始終是同一個實例。 Click 1 clickCount = 1 mouseDown self = 0xbb545ed00 (Button A) hitTest = Button A Click 2 clickCount = 2 mouseDown self = 0xbb545ed00 (Button A) hitTest = Button B Click 3 clickCount = 3 mouseDown self = 0xbb545ed00 (Button A) hitTest = Button B 這代表： 第一下點擊時，接收事件的是 Button A。 Cell 刪除並重新排版後，滑鼠下方已經變成 Button B（Hit Test 的結果）。 但後續點擊的 mouseDown，仍然由 Button A 接收。 畫面上滑鼠下方的 Button，和實際收到滑鼠事件的 Button，並不是同一個。 TODO（發文前請確認）：目前只觀察到現象，尚未確認 AppKit 為何在連續點擊時沿用舊的接收者，也沒驗證「停頓後恢復」是否與系統雙擊間隔有關。若有實測或文件佐證，請補在這裡；沒有的話，這段維持「觀察到的現象」即可。 在 Button 的 mouseDown 中判斷事件是否真的落在自己身上

items.title: Hallucinated Packages & Dependency Drift in AI-Assisted Code
items.summary: During a routine review on a client's Laravel and Vue project, one pull request added a Composer package with a perfectly reasonable name for parsing VAT numbers. The code looked fine and the tests passed locally for the author, because he had copied a helper from an assistant's answer and installed the package by hand. The CI build failed with "package not found". The package had never existed. The assistant had invented a plausible name. That time the failure was harmless. The worrying part is that anyone can register a missing name on a public registry, and attackers do watch for names that assistants tend to invent. I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every command against Composer 2.8, npm 10 and pnpm 9. items.title: Decompiling allows ref struct: the whole feature is one metadata bit, and dropping it silently narrows your contract
items.summary: Most C# language features leave a trail in the instruction stream. An async method becomes a state machine you can single-step; a yield return becomes a MoveNext with a jumped-to label; even a using is just a try/finally around a Dispose. A decompiler earns its keep by reading those instructions and folding them back into the syntax that produced them. The C# 13 allows ref struct anti-constraint is the opposite kind of feature. It produces no method-body IL whatsoever. The entire feature is one bit in one metadata table, set on one generic parameter. That makes it one of the cleanest case studies there is for why a decompiler has to read metadata as carefully as it reads code — because here the code says nothing, and a tool that only reads code will hand you source that compiles, runs identically, and is quietly wrong. This post walks the construct for Glass.NET, the free .NET decompiler. A normal generic constraint adds a requirement. where T : IDisposable says a type argument must implement IDisposable; the compiler enforces it, and the metadata records it as a row in the GenericParamConstraints table pointing at the IDisposable type. allows ref struct does the reverse. items.title: Building a Privacy-First Desktop OCR & Translation Pipeline for macOS: Deep Dive into Apple Vision Framework
items.summary: As developers and researchers, our desktop screens display our most sensitive intellectual property: uncommitted proprietary code, confidential game crash logs, private API keys, and draft academic papers. Yet, many popular desktop translation utilities take an alarming architectural shortcut: they capture your screen and ship the entire raw PNG/JPEG image directly to cloud-hosted computer vision APIs. In this technical breakdown, we explore how to build a Privacy-First Desktop OCR & Translation Architecture on macOS. By leveraging Apple's native Vision Framework and ScreenCaptureKit, we ensure that image frames never leave the user's local machine, while only sanitized textual tokens cross the network boundary. When an application asks for macOS Screen Recording permissions, it gains access to every pixel rendered on the display. En este artículo explico la parte de la aplicación: cómo modelamos los datos como documentos, cómo elegimos la clave de partición y qué consultas hace la API. 👉 App publicada: https://app-tacnago-geraldzvallos.azurewebsites.net Repositorio: https://github.com/Geraldzvallos/tacnago-cosmosdb Queríamos algo pequeño pero real: una lista de lugares de Tacna (historia, museos, playas, gastronomía, naturaleza y pueblos) que se pueda filtrar, buscar y ampliar desde la web. Es un buen caso para una base de datos de documentos, porque cada lugar tiene datos parecidos, pero no siempre los mismos. En una base relacional tendríamos que crear columnas para todo, o tablas aparte para los datos que solo algunos lugares tienen. En Cosmos DB for NoSQL cada lugar es un documento JSON y cada uno puede traer los campos que necesite. items.title: I shipped a VPN app on iOS, Mac, Android and Windows without writing a VPN protocol
items.summary: I build mobile apps for a living, mostly on iOS. This year I shipped a VPN called Privalune on iPhone, iPad, Mac, Android and Windows. I did it alone, and the only reason that was possible is one decision I made early: I would not write or bundle a VPN protocol. Every platform I target already ships an IKEv2 client. So the apps are remote controls. They hand the operating system a server and a login, and the OS runs the tunnel. This post covers how that works on each platform, what the backend looks like, and where the approach hurts. The numbers None of those codebases contains cryptography or packet handling. iOS and Mac: NEVPNManager On Apple platforms the system VPN is NEVPNManager, the "Personal VPN" API. You fill in an IKEv2 profile, save it, and ask the system to start it. iOS shows its own permission prompt the first time. The part I like most is on-demand rules. items.title: Manjaro Linux Moves Toward Independent Community Governance
items.summary: Arch-based Manjaro Linux "has announced that Manjaro Project e.V. is now officially registered as a non-profit in Germany," reports Linuxiac, "and is therefore a legally separate entity from the commercial Manjaro GmbH & Co. KG... after months of internal wrangling over who was in charge of the project, who had access to the infrastructure and who didn't, and the relationship between the dev team and the commercial company..." The restructuring goes back to March, when the Manjaro developers released the Manjaro 2.0 Manifesto, which was a very public critique of the way Manjaro was being run. But in January America's federal government launched a program called WISeR that uses AI to evaluate authorization requests for certain procedures from America's federal health insurance program for seniors, Medicare. EFF sued for records and discovered "additional issues" with the program that they say "could jeopardize Medicare beneficiaries' access to care." EFF has now published hundreds of pages of documents obtained through our lawsuit, available here... items.title: Linus Torvalds Wonders If Linux's AI-Prompted Patch Flood Has Peaked
items.summary: The Register writes that "The worst of the patchpocalypse may be behind us, according to Linus Torvalds." In his weekly kernel update post, Torvalds said Linux 7.4 rc2 was a big release partly because it contained code he'd left out of rc1 because he'd been busy and it was already the largest such release in kernel history. But Torvalds said the other reason rc2 was big was "various AI fixes." Such fixes are necessary because ever since Anthropic launched its Mythos bug-finding model in April, developers have been able to find more software flaws than was previously possible. Microsoft, for example, addressed a record 974 flaws in September — its third record fixing spree this year after it whacked 622 flaws in July and 206 in June. Oracle addressed 1,449 flaws in a single month. That's many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI. Torvalds' post suggests that, perhaps, the worst of this is behind us. items.title: Local Apple Vision OCR for uncopyable macOS errors and two-column PDFs
items.summary: The problem: the text exists, but you cannot select it On macOS, a lot of the text that blocks you is drawn, not selectable: Unity's console output (NullReferenceException: Object reference not set to an instance of an object) Blender's status/error dialogs (Error: Cannot read file "...": No such file or directory) Xcode's red inline diagnostics Gatekeeper and permission dialogs ("AppName" cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified.) Any English text baked into a screenshot or a scanned PDF Copy-paste translation pipelines fail on all of these, because there is no text layer to copy. And text-extraction order from a two-column PDF frequently interleaves the columns, so pasting into a translator produces scrambled sentences even when extraction succeeds. So the job is: read what is on screen, in place, without shipping the screenshot anywhere. The split I settled on: Stage Where it runs What leaves the machine Screen capture → text recognition On-device (Apple Vision, VNRecognizeTextRequest) nothing — pixels stay local Recognized text → translation Online the recognized string only This is deliberate. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman. That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely. But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. "These answers exist, but the only way to find them has been to leave Amazon for painstaking research on brand websites, third party review sites and tech forums." Reuters could not determine if or when this plan may be implemented, though the document, written like a press release, has an aspirational future release date of October 1, 2027. items.title: US university students tell surveillance cameras to Flock off
items.summary: The privacy issues over the company’s surveillance cameras have caused protests in schools all over the country Angela Nguyen, a senior at Stanford University, has been on a mission to make sure her school doesn’t use automated license plate readers, like those made by Flock Safety, for mass surveillance. The 21-year-old computer science major helped collect hundreds of signatures earlier this year from students, faculty, alumni and residents to demand that Stanford drop its current Flock contract and codify safeguards for similar tech tools the school may use in the future. The fear, Nguyen says, is that these cameras, which show where a vehicle was at a certain point in time, can be exploited to victimize vulnerable people. Stanford cut ties with Flock this summer, and it’s not alone. The privacy reckoning over the company’s surveillance cameras is gaining momentum at schools nationwide. Since April, at least ten university campuses across seven states, have scrapped contracts with Flock. items.title: Eliminating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference with Integer-Only Arithmetic (15 minute read)
items.summary: A floating-point number stores a fixed number of significant digits and a separate exponent. When two numbers with very different exponents are added, the small one has to be shifted to line up with the big one, and the digits that fall off on the end are gone. That means that (a+b)+c is not always equal to a+(b+c). This post looks at what happens when integer addition, which is exact, is used.

items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.

items.title: SpaceX's Starfall just went from secret to storefront (16 minute read)
items.summary: SpaceX has launched a commercial page for Starfall, a disk-shaped reentry capsule that can carry up to 1,000 kg of payload. items.title: The Stacks Project, formalized in Lean (13 minute read)
